atlas-pt.0119: Probation (período experimental) on a permanent contract is 90 days for most workers, 180 days for technically complex or highly responsible roles and 240 days for management; on fixed-term contracts it is 30 days from six months’ duration and 15 days below.
atlas-pt.0120: The 2019 reform’s 180 days for first-job seekers was declared unconstitutional by the Constitutional Court, but only for those previously on fixed-term contracts with other employers of 90 days or more.
atlas-pt.0121: Portuguese pay is 14 salaries: a holiday subsidy and a Christmas subsidy, the latter due by 15 December, are paid on top of the 12 months, and both can be paid in monthly instalments. Holiday is at least 22 working days a year.
atlas-pt.0122: A permanent employee resigns with 30 days’ notice up to two years of seniority and 60 days above; BPI’s trainee programme starts on an open-ended contract, while Novobanco’s is a 9-month paid project. Pay is usually raised in the first interview, not after the offer.
atlas-pt.0123: The residence visa for subordinate work requires a work contract or a promise of one, or recognised qualifications and an individual expression of interest from the employer (Lei 23/2007, art. 59 n.º 5); the article does not set a quota or labour-market test, so ask for the contract or promise early.
atlas-pt.0124: Highly qualified work needs a contract of at least six months at a minimum pay set in the law (art. 61-A), so raise the permit at the offer stage.
atlas-pt.0125: Most graduate programmes read do not state a nationality rule; Novobanco and BPI make Portuguese mandatory, Jerónimo Martins asks for fluent Portuguese and English, and EDP says Portuguese is not required.
atlas-pt.0126: Nova SBE’s career fair, with 43 organisations from 50 markets and an international focus, and Landing.jobs, which offers visa and relocation help, are where employers used to hiring across borders are easiest to find.
atlas-pt.0127: Posted vacancies: Net-Empregos (61,690 active offers on 8 October 2026), the IEFP portal for job offers and registration, and Landing.jobs for tech.
atlas-pt.0128: Graduate programmes and fairs: Talent Portugal lists trainee programmes (BPI, Novobanco) and a fair calendar; the employers’ own pages carry EDP, Galp, Jerónimo Martins and Sonae.
atlas-pt.0129: University fairs: Técnico’s Jobshop (April), the Nova SBE Career Fair (September 2026) and Católica’s RUMO in Porto (November).
atlas-pt.0130: Public sector: competition notices appear in full on the Bolsa de Emprego Público (BEP) and as an extract in the Diário da República.
atlas-pt.0131: Missing the window: BPI opened in February and March, Sonae closed on 6 April, Novobanco ran 20 April to 14 June, and the state internship runs only 12 October to 7 December 2026.
atlas-pt.0132: Applying to a programme where Portuguese is mandatory without it, or assuming English is enough: only EDP says so, and Jerónimo Martins asks for fluent Portuguese and English.
atlas-pt.0133: Sending one generic CV: E-Konomista lists generic CVs, unexplained gaps, keyword stuffing and an objective statement as errors, and recommends a summary of 3 to 4 lines tailored to each application.
atlas-pt.0134: Treating the odds of a big programme as normal: Jerónimo Martins took 11 people from more than 1,400 applications in 2025, so apply to several programmes and keep the internship route open.
atlas-pt.0135: Arriving late: punctuality is a must at work in Portugal even if time is relaxed in personal life.
atlas-pt.0136: BPI asks for a proficient command of English and makes Portuguese mandatory; Novobanco’s online tests include language proficiency and Portuguese is mandatory.
atlas-pt.0137: Jerónimo Martins asks for fluent Portuguese and English; EDP’s Global Graduate Program is the exception, saying Portuguese is not required.
atlas-pt.0138: The foreign engineering hubs in Lisbon and the Landing.jobs platform advertise across Europe, so English is often enough there; Novobanco’s technology profile still lists Portuguese as mandatory.
atlas-pt.0139: Public competitions are published in Portuguese in the Diário da República and on the BEP, and the selection runs in Portuguese; expect to need it.
atlas-pt.0140: The 38% of IEFP interns in work within 12 months (16% at the same firm) is from a 2016 evaluation, before the current +Talento scheme, and is the only conversion figure found.
atlas-pt.0141: In 2025, 83.9% of Portuguese tertiary graduates aged 20 to 34 who left education up to three years earlier were in work, against 85.3% in the EU, while unemployment among under-25s was 19.8% in August 2026.
atlas-pt.0142: Nova SBE’s 100% employment at three months comes with 93% international students and a high mobility rank, so it does not measure staying in Portugal; no source read gives the share of programme graduates who stay.
atlas-pt.0143: EU, EEA and Swiss citizens need no visa or work authorisation, and enter with a passport or identity card.
atlas-pt.0144: After three months, register within the following 30 days at the town hall (Câmara Municipal) for the EU registration certificate (CRUE), valid five years.
atlas-pt.0145: Get a tax number (NIF) first: you need it for a contract, a lease and a bank account. EU residents need no tax representative.
atlas-pt.0146: Higher-education student visa (D4) and residence permit
atlas-pt.0147: Get the D4 visa at a consulate before you travel; it carries your appointment with the migration agency AIMA, where you receive the residence permit.
atlas-pt.0148: Students may work, employed or self-employed, with no fixed cap on hours as long as the work stays secondary to studying; no separate authorisation is needed.
atlas-pt.0149: A non-EU student with a student permit from another EU country can study here up to 360 days with no visa, once AIMA is notified.
atlas-pt.0150: €920 a month (€11,040 a year); €460 with housing secured
atlas-pt.0154: An internship outside a degree must pay a monthly grant set by your qualification, plus a meal allowance for each day worked and accident insurance; it lasts up to nine months.
atlas-pt.0155: Non-EU interns need a temporary-stay or residence visa for internship; with a job offer at the end, the permit converts to work without leaving Portugal.
atlas-pt.0158: Job-search or business permit after a Portuguese degree
atlas-pt.0159: After a master’s or doctorate in Portugal you can get 12 months with no consular visa, free to work, registered with the job centre (IEFP); a stable job converts it to a work permit inside Portugal.
atlas-pt.0160: Graduates, bachelor’s included, with a job offer before their student permit ends can switch straight to a work permit.
atlas-pt.0162: AIMA fees, applying without a visa
atlas-pt.0165: The old open job-seeker visa was abolished; its replacement for listed skills is not yet issued, because the implementing order has not been published.
atlas-pt.0166: A contract of at least six months; a three-year degree, or experience (three years in the last seven for IT, five otherwise). Your family can join at once, and after a year you can move to another EU country more easily.
atlas-pt.0168: Salary, shortage jobs or recent graduates
atlas-pt.0171: €329.70 at the desk, plus the €110 visa
atlas-pt.0172: Highly qualified work visa (D3) and Tech Visa
atlas-pt.0173: A contract of at least a year in a specialist role, a degree or five years of experience, and pay of at least 1.5 times the national average or three times the social index. Companies certified by IAPMEI can use the Tech Visa, which gets the visa in about 15 to 20 days.
atlas-pt.0174: Pay floor (three times the social index)
atlas-pt.0177: A contract of at least a year at no less than the minimum wage, with the job first offered through the employment institute (IEFP). The first permit lasts two years, then three; after five years, permanent residence or citizenship.
atlas-pt.0179: A hosting agreement with a research centre or university accredited by FCT or DGES; priority visa handling, family reunion at once and mobility within the EU.
atlas-pt.0180: FCT doctoral grants are free of income tax, and FCT pays your voluntary social-security contributions.
atlas-pt.0181: Portugal has no working-holiday agreement with the UK or the US.
atlas-pt.0182: Only for citizens of Australia, New Zealand, Japan, South Korea, Canada, Argentina, Chile, Peru and Uruguay aged 18 to 30 (35 for Canada): 12 months, work for six at most, and no conversion inside Portugal.
atlas-pt.0183: Up to 90 days in any 180, with no work. Arriving through another Schengen country and not staying in a hotel, send an entry declaration to AIMA or the police within three working days; missing it costs €60 to €190.
atlas-pt.0184: Since June 2024 you can no longer arrive as a tourist and apply for residence on the spot: a consular visa first is the only way.
atlas-pt.0186: The five years towards citizenship count from the day you applied for your first residence permit, so AIMA’s delays do not cost you time.
atlas-pt.0188: Workers up to 35 pay no income tax in their first year, then 75%, 50% and 25% of it is exempt over ten years, on up to €29,542.15 a year.
